day-1.t: Day 1 — A job description that does the filtering for you

b.v: Today's goal

v: Write a job description that filters out the wrong people
Separate must-have from nice-to-have
Stop scaring away good candidates with a wish list

b.v: About 20 minutes. Use a real role you need to fill. Running example: Karim Traders in Multan, 12 staff, hiring a Sales and Dispatch Officer at Rs 65,000 a month.

Most small-company job ads are a wish list copied from a big company: five years of experience, a degree, Excel, Photoshop, driving licence, willing to travel, salary negotiable. They attract everyone and filter nobody, so you read 90 CVs to find four people worth calling. A good ad is written to make unsuitable people decide not to apply.
1) Separate must-have from nice-to-have
A must-have is something you cannot teach in three months and cannot work around. Everything else is nice-to-have. Most roles have three or four must-haves, not twelve.

v: Must-have = can read and write English and Urdu well enough for customer messages
Must-have = has handled order booking and dispatch for a trading or retail business
Must-have = can travel to the market area three days a week
Nice-to-have = a business degree
Nice-to-have = knows our accounting software
Nice-to-have should be written as nice-to-have, so a strong candidate without it still applies

b.v: 2) Write the ad in this order
Candidates read the first three lines and decide. Put the work and the money early, and the company story at the end where it belongs.

Write five sections:|Title and one line: Sales and Dispatch Officer, Karim Traders, Multan|What the job actually is, in 3 bullets: take orders on WhatsApp and phone, prepare dispatch slips, follow up with delivery riders|What you must have, in 3 bullets only|What you will get: Rs 65,000 a month, one weekly off, lunch, fuel for market visits|How to apply: send a WhatsApp message to this number with your name, area and last job. No CV needed for the first step
3) Add one line that filters by itself
A single specific instruction removes most of the noise. People who cannot follow a simple instruction in the ad will not follow instructions in the job. This is the cheapest filter ever invented.

v: Example filter = start your message with the word DISPATCH
Example filter = tell me the area of Multan you live in and how you would travel to work
Example filter = answer one real question: a customer ordered 3 cartons, we have 2. What do you tell them?
Result = you can delete half the replies without reading them, and the half you keep has already shown something

b.v: The most common beginner mistake is writing salary negotiable. It attracts everyone and wastes your time on people whose minimum is far above your budget. State the range or the exact figure. The wrong people will not apply, which is the point.
Practice

Write the ad for your real role in five sections, with exactly three must-haves and one filter instruction. Then read it as a candidate would: does it say what the person will do on a normal Tuesday? If it only says what you hope they are like, rewrite the second section.

day-2.t: Day 2 — Sourcing where good people actually are

b.v: Today's goal

v: Build four sourcing channels you can use repeatedly
Ask for referrals in a way that produces names
Keep a warm list even when you are not hiring

b.v: About 20 minutes. Make a list of ten people you could ask for a name today.

Sourcing means finding candidates before they find you. Small companies usually post one ad and wait. That gives you whoever happens to be looking that week, which is rarely the best person. The strongest hires usually come through a person who already knows your work.
1) Four channels, in order of value
Start with the channels that cost nothing and give context, and only then pay for advertising.

v: Referrals = your current staff, suppliers, customers. Best quality, because someone vouches for the person
Direct approach = you already know someone good at a competitor or a neighbouring business
Local groups = trade WhatsApp groups, area Facebook groups, college notice boards, mosque or community announcements
Job boards = useful for office roles and for reach, but you will read more unsuitable applications

b.v: 2) Ask for referrals properly
Can you think of anyone means no. A specific question with a name and a reason produces names. Ask three people today with the same sentence.

Use this wording:|I am hiring a dispatch officer in Multan, around Rs 65,000, mostly market visits and order follow-up.|Who is the most reliable person you have worked with in dispatch, even if they are not looking right now?|If they join and stay three months, I will give you Rs 5,000 as a thank you.|May I use your name when I contact them?

v: Say the salary, so the referral is realistic
Say the referral bonus up front, and pay it on time. It protects your reputation
Ask for one name, not a list. One name gets thought, a list gets guesses

b.v: 3) Keep a warm list all year
The worst time to look for people is when someone resigns. Keep a simple list of people you would hire if a seat opened, and stay in light contact. Three messages a year is enough.

v: Name, role, where they work now, how they were rated when you met them
One line on why you would hire them
A yes or no on whether they would move for the right offer
A date you last spoke. Anyone untouched for a year is cold, not warm

b.v: Do not promise a job to someone to keep them warm. If you say there is a seat for you in March and March arrives with no seat, you have lost that person and their whole circle. Say there is no seat today, and that you would like to stay in touch.
Practice
Write the referral message in your own words and send it to three people today. Then start the warm list with five names, including one person you cannot hire now but would hire later.
Today's goal

v: Score candidates against the must-haves only
Cut your review time without missing good people
Keep a short record of why each person was or was not called

b.v: About 20 minutes. Bring 10 real applications if you have them, or invent a set.

Fair shortlisting is not only a legal and ethical matter, it is also the fastest way to hire well. When you score everyone against the same written criteria, you stop being swayed by a confident voice or a familiar university, and you can explain your decision months later if anyone asks.
1) Score three criteria, one to five
Use only the must-haves from the job description. Three criteria, scored one to five, is enough for a first cut and takes two minutes per candidate.

Shortlist like this:|Criterion A: relevant dispatch or order-handling experience. 1 none, 5 three or more years|Criterion B: written communication in the language the job needs. Judge from their message, not their CV font|Criterion C: practical fit, meaning travel, area, availability|Add the three scores. Call everyone scoring 10 or more|For anyone below 10, write one line saying why. That is your record
2) Review in two passes, not one
The first pass is fast and shallow. The second is careful and only for a short list. Doing both at once is what makes reviewing 90 applications take a whole weekend.

v: Pass one, 15 seconds each = did they follow the filter instruction, and do they meet at least one must-have?
Pass two, 3 minutes each = for survivors only, score the three criteria and check for anything alarming
Never = read a whole CV before checking the filter. You will feel obliged to the person and start making excuses for them

b.v: Do not shortlist on things that have nothing to do with the work: the neighbourhood someone lives in, their gender, their age, whether they are married, or a photograph. It is unfair, it is often unlawful, and it makes you hire worse. Score the must-haves and nothing else.
3) Keep a one-page record

Write down the name, the date, the three scores and one line of reason. If a rejected candidate asks why, you can answer in one sentence without guessing. If a future manager asks how you chose, the record answers.

v: Name and date received
Three scores and the total
Called yes or no, with a one-line reason
Kept on file yes or no, for future roles

b.v: Practice

Score ten real or sample applications on the three criteria and rank them. Then check yourself: is the top of your list the person with the best evidence, or the person with the nicest CV formatting? If the second, rescore before you call anyone.

day-4.t: Day 4 — Structured interviews that predict the job

b.v: Today's goal

v: Ask the same five questions to every candidate
Use past behaviour instead of opinions
Score answers so the decision is not just a feeling

b.v: About 25 minutes. Write your five questions before you read the rest of the lesson.

An unstructured interview is a conversation that tells you whether you enjoy talking to someone. That is not the same as whether they will do the job. Structured interviews ask the same questions in the same order and score the answers, which makes them far better at predicting performance and far fairer to quiet candidates.
1) Ask for a past example, not an opinion

Tell me about yourself invites a rehearsed speech. Tell me about a time you… invites evidence. The format is simple: situation, what they did, what happened. If they cannot give a real example, that is information.

Use this five-question set for the dispatch role:|Tell me about a time a customer said an order had not arrived. What did you do, step by step?|Describe a day when three orders had to go out and only two riders were available.|Tell me about a mistake you made in a dispatch or stock record. What happened next?|How do you keep track of 20 open orders without dropping one? Walk me through it.|What did your last supervisor ask you to improve, and what did you change?

v: Listen for I did, not we did. Probe once: what was your part exactly?
Ask what happened next. The result is where the real answer is
Silence is allowed. Let them think for five seconds instead of filling the gap
Never ask about family plans, religion, caste, political views or health

b.v: 2) Score each answer one to four
Score immediately after each answer, not at the end of the day. Memory flattens everyone into a vague yes after four interviews. Write the number and one word of evidence.

v: 1 = no example, or an answer about opinions only
2 = a vague example with no clear action from them
3 = a clear example with a sensible action and a result
4 = a clear example with judgement, a trade-off they saw, and a measurable result

b.v: Do not fill the interview by talking about yourself for 20 minutes. Nervous candidates relax when you talk, and you leave knowing nothing. Talk for two minutes at the start, then listen for the rest.
3) Let them interview you too

Always leave five minutes for their questions, and answer honestly, including the boring parts. A person who understands the job and still wants it is worth far more than one who was sold a dream and leaves in month two.

Close every interview the same way:|What questions do you have for me?|Say the next step and the date: we will call by Thursday either way|Say the salary again, clearly, so there is no surprise later|Thank them and walk them out. Do not discuss them in the corridor while they can hear
Practice

Write your five questions and a scorecard with a 1 to 4 scale. Then run a 20-minute practice interview with a friend and score them honestly. You will find one question that produces nothing useful. Replace it now, before real candidates arrive.

day-5.t: Day 5 — Reference checks, offers and probation

b.v: Today's goal

v: Check references in ten minutes and learn something real
Write an offer letter that prevents arguments
Use probation honestly, with a date and a decision

b.v: About 20 minutes. Have your interview notes nearby.

A reference check is not a formality. It is the one place where someone who has actually worked with your candidate will tell you the thing the candidate did not. And an offer letter is not paperwork, it is the shared understanding that stops month-two disputes about salary, hours and duties.
1) Ask three questions that get real answers
Most referees are polite and guarded. Ask specific questions, and ask for a comparison, because comparisons are harder to answer with a compliment.

Run the call:|Confirm the dates they worked together and the role|On a scale of one to ten, how would you rate their reliability? Then: what would make it a nine?|Tell me about one time they handled a difficult customer or a mistake|Would you hire them again for the same role? If there is a pause, ask why|Thank them and confirm you will not quote them by name to the candidate

v: Ask for a work reference, not a family friend, whenever possible
Two references is enough for a small company
Write two lines of what you heard, dated. It is part of the hiring record
If a referee is enthusiastic but vague, that is a soft warning, not a pass

b.v: 2) The offer letter, in plain language
One page, no legal fog. State exactly what was agreed, because most early disputes are about something both sides thought was obvious.

Include these eight items:|Job title and who they report to|Start date, working days and hours, and the weekly off|Salary in rupees, how it is paid, and the payment date each month|Any allowances, separately and clearly|Probation period and the salary during probation|Notice required from either side during and after probation|Leave entitlement, stated as days per year|That the appointment is subject to the company's rules, and that local labour law applies. Ask a qualified professional to review the wording before you use it

Do not copy an offer letter from the internet and use it as your contract. Employment terms, notice, leave and termination rules differ by province and change over time. Have a local labour lawyer or a registered HR consultant review your template once. This course cannot give you legal advice.
3) Make probation a real decision date
Probation without a review is just a lower salary for three months. Set the review date in the letter, diarise it, and decide on the day.

v: Write three things the person must be doing independently by the end of probation
Review at the halfway point, not only at the end
At the end, decide: confirm, extend once with written reasons, or end it properly
Tell them the decision on the date you promised. Silence is a decision too, and the wrong one

b.v: Practice

Write your offer letter template with the eight items, leaving placeholders for name, date and salary. Then write the three probation success statements for your role. Send the template to a labour lawyer or HR professional for a paid review before you next hire.

day-6.t: Day 6 — Onboarding: the first day, week and month

b.v: Today's goal

v: Prepare the first day so nobody sits idle
Run a 30-60-90 day plan
Cut the early-quit risk in the first two weeks

b.v: About 20 minutes. Build the checklist even if your next hire is months away.

People rarely quit in month six because of the work. They quit in month two because nobody told them where things are, who to ask, or whether they were doing well. Onboarding is the cheapest retention tool you have, and it costs preparation, not money.
1) The first day, hour by hour

A new person's first day should answer three questions: where do I sit, what do I do first, who do I ask? If they spend the first day waiting, they conclude the company is disorganised, and they are right.

Prepare before they arrive:|The day before: desk or counter space ready, chair, any tools, a notebook and pen|Hour one: welcome, tea, introductions to every person by name and role|Hour two: walk the premises. Stock room, washroom, first aid, where to park|Hour three: sit with a colleague and watch the work being done|End of day: 15 minutes with the owner. What surprised you? What do you need tomorrow?

v: Give them one small real task on day one that they can finish. Finishing something matters more than watching
Name one buddy, a person they can ask a silly question without embarrassment
Give the phone numbers they need, written down, including yours
Do not leave them alone on day one, even for two hours

b.v: 2) The 30-60-90 plan
Write it with the new person in week one. Three columns, one page, and a review at each 30-day line. It turns a vague hope into visible progress.

v: Days 1 to 30 = learn. Shadow, do the task with help, learn the product names and the customers
Days 31 to 60 = do. Own the routine with checks. Handle normal problems alone
Days 61 to 90 = improve. Fix one recurring problem, and train or guide someone else on one task
Each stage needs one measurable statement, for example: by day 60, dispatch slips are prepared without checking with me

b.v: Do not hand a new person the hardest customer or the month-end close in their first week and call it a test. Failing early teaches them they cannot ask for help. Give a real but survivable task, and be nearby.
3) The two-week check-in
Twenty minutes at the end of week two, with four questions. This is where you find the small problems while they are still small.

Ask these four:|What is harder than you expected?|What have you not been told that you needed?|Who has helped you most, and who has been hard to reach?|Is there anything about the job that is not what you expected?
Practice

Write your onboarding checklist with at least 15 items across first day, first week and 30-60-90. Then write the day-one small real task for your role. If you cannot name a task a beginner can finish on day one, the role needs restructuring before you hire.

day-7.t: Day 7 — Contracts and records you must keep

b.v: Today's goal

v: Know which documents every employee must have
Build one simple personal file per person
Understand clearly when you must pay a professional

b.v: About 20 minutes. This lesson is about organisation, not legal advice.

Small companies get into trouble not because they are dishonest, but because nothing is written down. When a dispute arrives two years later, memory is not evidence. A thin, complete file for each person solves most of it.
1) The documents every employee should have
Exact requirements depend on your province, your industry and the size of your business, and they change. Treat this as a starting list to confirm with a professional, not as the final word.

v: A written appointment letter or contract, signed and dated by both sides
A copy of the employee's identity document
Two references with contact details
Emergency contact name and number
Job description, one page, signed
Any qualification or experience certificates you relied on when hiring
Records of salary paid, with dates and amounts
Leave taken and leave balance

b.v: 2) One file per person, paper or digital
Keep it in one place, locked, with access limited to you and one other named person. Salary and identity documents are private, and staff talk about who can see what.

Set up the file system:|One folder per person, named Surname-Firstname-StaffNumber|Inside: contract, identity copy, references, job description, salary record, leave record|Put a one-page summary sheet on top: start date, role, salary, probation end date, next review date|Keep a simple index of who has which file, in case of an inspection or a dispute|Review every six months and remove what you no longer need, keeping what the law requires

Never keep only a WhatsApp conversation as your record of salary, notice or leave. Screenshots get lost, phones get replaced, and message history disappears. Write the decision on paper or in a document, then send the message.
3) When to pay a professional, without hesitation

This course can tell you how to be organised. It cannot tell you what the law requires, because that depends on your province, your sector, your headcount and the current rules. Getting it wrong can cost far more than the advice.

v: Consult a labour lawyer = before you draft a contract, a termination letter, or a policy on fines and deductions
Consult a tax or payroll professional = before you set up salary deductions, tax withholding or any statutory contribution
Consult an accountant = before you change how you record wages or pay anyone off the books
Ask the question in writing, keep the reply, and date it. Advice you cannot show later is half advice

b.v: Practice

List every current employee and tick which documents you actually hold. Most people find two or three gaps. Fix one gap today by asking for the missing paper, and write the review date for the whole set in your calendar.

day-8.t: Day 8 — Payroll: what you must understand even if someone else runs it

b.v: Today's goal

v: Read a payslip and explain every line
Run a simple, repeatable monthly payroll routine
Know exactly which parts need a tax professional

b.v: About 20 minutes. If you already pay salaries, keep last month's numbers in front of you.

You do not need to be a payroll expert to run a small company. You do need to know what each deduction is, so that nobody can quietly take money that is not theirs, and so that your staff trust their payslip. Trust in pay is the foundation of everything else.
1) The parts of a payslip
Every payslip is a small subtraction: what was earned, minus what is deducted, equals what is paid. Learn the four blocks and you can read any of them.

v: Earnings = basic salary, allowances, overtime if you pay it, bonus
Gross pay = all earnings added together
Deductions = anything subtracted, such as absence, an advance repayment, or a statutory deduction required by law
Net pay = gross minus deductions. This is the amount that must actually reach the person

b.v: 2) A worked example, with arithmetic you can check
Bilal earns Rs 65,000 a month: Rs 55,000 basic and Rs 10,000 travel allowance. He took two unpaid days, and he is repaying a Rs 10,000 advance at Rs 2,500 a month.

Do the sum in this order:|Gross pay: 55,000 + 10,000 = Rs 65,000|Daily rate for absence: 65,000 divided by 26 working days = Rs 2,500|Two unpaid days: 2 × 2,500 = Rs 5,000|Advance repayment: Rs 2,500|Total deductions before any statutory amount: 5,000 + 2,500 = Rs 7,500|Net pay: 65,000 − 7,500 = Rs 57,500|Now apply any tax or statutory deduction required by current law, as advised by your tax professional, and record it separately on the payslip

v: Show the advance balance after repayment, so there is no argument next month
Split basic and allowances clearly, because some statutory calculations use basic only
Never make a deduction that is not written in the contract or agreed in writing
Give a payslip every month, even a WhatsApp message with the four numbers

b.v: Do not calculate income tax, social security or any statutory contribution from a course or a blog post. Rates, thresholds and rules change, and they differ by province and by employment type. Get the current figures from a qualified tax practitioner, in writing, and keep the note in your payroll file.
3) A monthly routine that never slips
Payroll goes wrong when it is done in a rush on the last day. A fixed routine, started a week early, removes almost all of the risk.

Run payroll on the same dates every month:|Day 20: collect attendance, leave and any advance requests|Day 22: calculate gross, deductions and net for each person. Prepare the bank or wallet transfer list|Day 24: check the total against your budget, and get one other person to check the arithmetic|Day 25 to 28: pay, and send each payslip|Day 28: file the payroll sheet and the transfer proof together|After paying: collect signed acknowledgements for cash payments
Practice

Build a payslip template with earnings, gross, each deduction, net and the advance balance. Run Bilal's numbers through it and confirm you get Rs 57,500 before any statutory deduction. Then write your payroll calendar dates in your phone for the next three months.
Today's goal

v: Hold a monthly 20-minute one-to-one
Give feedback that changes behaviour
Handle a real performance problem in a documented way

b.v: About 20 minutes. Think of one person whose work has slipped.

Most managers in small companies only talk to staff when something is wrong. That makes every conversation feel like a warning, so people hide problems and you hear about them late. A short monthly conversation, in good months and bad, changes the whole relationship.
1) The 20-minute monthly one-to-one
Four questions, in this order, twenty minutes, once a month, same day. Do not cancel it. Cancelling teaches people that the conversation is not real.

Run it like this:|What went well this month? Let them answer first, and be specific back|What got in your way? Listen for process problems, which are usually yours to fix|What do you want to get better at in the next month? Agree one thing, not five|What do you need from me? Write the answer, and do it before the next meeting

v: Write two lines afterwards: what was agreed, and the date you will check
Praise in public, correct in private
One improvement focus at a time. Five at once is none
If the person says everything is fine and you know it is not, ask a smaller question: what is the most annoying part of your week?

b.v: 2) Feedback that can be acted on
Vague feedback creates defensiveness because there is nothing to fix. Specific feedback about a moment creates a change, because the person can see the moment you mean.

v: Weak = you need to be more careful with orders
Strong = on Tuesday, the Faisalabad order went out with 2 cartons instead of 3, and the customer called twice. Walk me through how you checked it
Structure = the moment, what happened, the effect, then a question that makes them think
Then agree the fix: a checklist, a second pair of eyes, or a different sequence

b.v: Do not save up six months of complaints and deliver them all in one meeting. It feels efficient and it feels, to the other person, like an ambush. They will remember the volume, not the content, and they will start looking for another job that week.
3) When it is a real performance problem

Sometimes the person cannot or will not do the job. Then you need a clear, written, time-bound process, and you need professional advice before you act. This is the area where small companies most often create a dispute for themselves.

Follow a documented sequence:|Write down the specific problem, with dates and examples. Facts, not adjectives|Meet, explain, and agree what good looks like, in writing|Set a review date, usually two to four weeks|Give the support the plan needs: training, time, tools|At the review, record the outcome honestly: improved, partly improved, or not improved|Before any warning, unpaid suspension, deduction or termination, take advice from a labour lawyer and follow your contract and the applicable law
Practice

Book a 20-minute one-to-one with each person who reports to you, in the next seven days. Write the four questions on a card. Then write one piece of specific feedback for one person, using the moment-effect-question structure, and deliver it this week.
Today's goal

v: Handle a resignation calmly and legally
Get a real handover instead of a messy one
Close the file properly and learn from the exit

b.v: About 20 minutes. Write your handover template, even if nobody is leaving.

How people leave is remembered longer than how they were hired. A good exit protects your customers, your records and your reputation in a small market where everyone knows everyone. It also protects you from disputes about final pay and company property.
1) The first hour after a resignation
Stay calm, thank them, and ask for it in writing. Nothing else in that first conversation. Anger in that hour costs you a clean handover.

Do this in order:|Ask for the resignation in writing, with the date and the last working day|Check the notice period in the contract and confirm it in writing|Tell them you will respond within two days, and do|Do not argue about salary or accuse them of disloyalty in the room|Tell the rest of the team only what is necessary, only after the person knows

Never hold back earned salary as leverage, or deduct for tools or training without a written basis. Withholding pay to force behaviour is one of the fastest ways to turn a normal resignation into a legal complaint. Take advice before any deduction from final pay.
2) A handover that actually transfers knowledge
Knowledge leaves with the person unless you schedule it out of them. Two weeks of a written list beats a fond farewell email.

Build the handover list:|Every task they do, and how often|Every file, folder and password they control, with the new owner named|Every external contact: suppliers, customers, riders, government offices|Every open item and its exact status|A named person who has watched each task being done at least once

v: Have them train the successor, not just write notes
Change every password on their last day, and check that it worked
Collect keys, cards, laptop, phone and uniform against a signed list
Keep a copy of the handover document in the personnel file

b.v: 3) Final settlement and the exit conversation

Final pay, leave balance and any dues must follow the contract and the law, and the law varies. Get the calculation checked by your accountant or a labour professional. Then close the file and ask three questions.

v: Settlement = salary up to the last day, unpaid leave balance, any agreed dues, minus documented and lawful deductions
Get a signed acknowledgement of full and final settlement, reviewed by your professional
Exit conversation = why did you decide to leave, what would have made you stay, would you recommend us to a friend
Write the honest answer in one line. Three exits with the same answer is a pattern, and patterns are fixable

b.v: Practice

Write your handover template with the five sections and the acknowledgement list. Then write the three exit questions on a card and keep it with your personnel files. The next time someone resigns, you will be calm and prepared instead of reactive.
